cards.a: All devices share a single transmission medium, originally a coaxial cable (10BASE2/10BASE5 'thicknet'/'thinnet'). Every frame travels the whole cable and every node sees it, giving one shared collision domain and one broadcast domain.

cards.q: How were nodes physically attached on a 10BASE2 bus versus a 10BASE5 bus?
cards.a: 10BASE2 used BNC T-connectors daisy-chained on the cable; 10BASE5 used 'vampire taps' that clamped onto the thick coax.

cards.q: What protocol arbitrated media access on a bus topology, and what did it mean for the collision domain?
cards.a: CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) arbitrated access. All nodes were in a single shared collision domain, so only one could transmit at a time.

cards.q: What is the purpose of terminators on a bus segment, and what happens if one is missing?
cards.a: Terminators at both ends of the cable absorb signals. If a terminator is missing, signals reflect back and the network appears 'gone'/down.

cards.q: What are the characteristics of a bus topology regarding collision domain, broadcast domain, and bandwidth?
cards.a: One collision domain (all nodes share it) and one broadcast domain; bandwidth is shared so all nodes divide the 10 Mbps. Security is weak because every node can see all traffic (promiscuous capture).

cards.q: Why did the bus topology fall out of use?
cards.a: It had a single point of failure (any cable break kills the whole segment), poor fault isolation, security exposure, scalability limits, and half-duplex on a shared medium. It was replaced by twisted-pair star wiring to switches.

cards.q: How does the bus concept relate to modern switching regarding hubs and switches?
cards.a: A hub recreates a bus because all its nodes share one collision domain. A switch microsegments so each port is its own collision domain. The exam treats 'bus equals one shared collision domain' as the definition of the model.

cards.q: A bus topology is one collision domain. What else is it in terms of domains?
cards.a: It is also one broadcast domain (unless separated by many VLANs).

cards.q: What happens to a bus when the cable breaks?
cards.a: A cable break splits the bus and can bring the whole segment down; a short can take the entire segment down. This is the classic argument for getting rid of bus topologies.

cards.q: Does CSMA/CD exist on switched full-duplex links?
cards.a: No. CSMA/CD is the media-arbitration protocol of bus/half-duplex shared media and does not exist on switched full-duplex links.

cards.q: In the bus Quick Review, what are the classic media and fault-isolation details?
cards.a: Media is a single shared coax cable (10BASE2/5). A cable break equals segment down — the worst fault isolation. Bandwidth is shared 10 Mbps that everyone divides, and it is legacy, appearing only in historical questions.
